questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That it was in China.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Hard because Tsinghua doesn't send out a lot of information until about a month or two before the exchange starts

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The check-in process was long but well executed.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: AB rooms (your own room and your share bathroom with one other person) and double rooms, because the single room dorm was under renovation.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: None in my building. Only a microwave, but they're very strict with what other electronic devices you have in your room. You can buy a mini fridge though.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Electronic devices can only be like up to 1000W i think, and has to be checked by the staff. They might take your electronic devices if it's too much and store it until the end of the semester.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had the AB room but no roommate so basically a single room. The building was old, so not the best facility but they are about to renovate it.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You just go to building 23 and there are students there to help you through the process.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Students were there to register you and the staff at the buildings were also helpful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Not too successful. There are multiple course lists that you can look at but they won't reflect the actual list of courses you can choose. So some courses I was interested in weren't there. I had to register classes the day after I arrived, and there wasn't much help with figuring out the school website. It was bugging for me for some time because you need the school's VPN to enter the domain, and it wouldn't always connect. So on the class registration start it's first come first. And there are limited spots on the classes and also limited classes offered in English. But it works out because the first week of classes is like a "trial" (even the teacher's treat it like that), and you can drop/register classes the week after or something. And sometimes the teachers open up more spaces in a class so more people can register (if you ask them or write to them).

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Look at the course lists before/in good time and plan the courses you think you'll take (plan more in case some aren't available). Make some friends on the first day of arriving so you can sit together when you register classes. You'll be in some Wechat groups. In my case someone took the initiative to go out on the first night and get to know each other. If you live in a double room, you could register with your roommate.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Most of my classes were Master's level. A lot of my friends were BA students and they said they could tell the level was higher. But in my opinion it's manageable.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It has much more of a classroom feel, like in high school. So participation in a lot of the classes gives extra points towards your final grade.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Natural language processing, web information retrieval, fundamentals of computer graphics, management of technological innovation, leadership and communication, elementary chinese A.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Depends on what you're studying, but for compsci I liked fundamentals of computer graphics and web IR, they were fun and you get to do some fun projects. Of other courses I recommend leadership and communication since the classes were interesting and I formed a tight group (you had to do a lot of group work in the same group).

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: You had to pay a student insurance (i think it was 600rmb). Also I didn't fill out the expenses for local transportation and personal spending, because technically you can stay within Tsinghua and not pay for local transportation. Subway and busses are super cheap, like a few RMB for a trip. Taxis (didi) are also fairly cheap so I used that a lot. Personal spendings is up to you and your own budget. I spend a lot on shopping (especially on taobao). And travelling is very doable during the semester.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Eating at restaurants (that arent like a local stall) was a bit more expensive than I thought. I can be like eating out in Denmark (like 100-200)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Didn't join any clubs because it didn't make sense to me to do it when I was only there for 1 semester. But I did go to some ice skating practice that was done by an ice skating club.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are many sports facilities and opportunities to join that. It's a thing at Tsinghua to work out too so they're big on it. Social activities is something planned by students. There was something called "pyro tuesday" where every tuesday there would be a party at a pizza spot that would turn into a bar that day.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Travelling! China is so big and has so much to offer. After all the travelling I did around China, I definitely felt that Beijing was somewhat boring at the end compared to other cities.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Travel. But don't forget to also explore Beijing. Or go to parties or clubs with friends.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I don't think you adjust much to the local culture since I feel like the culture at Tsinghua/at any university during an exchange will differ from "authentic" local culture a bit. You're surrounded by other exchange students so it feels more international in a way.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It's a bit hard because there's kind of a division between local and international students where each group keeps to themselves. It's just easier to connect with other international students because a lot of local students aren't the best at English.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not really

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The culture inside Tsinghua was very open, as everyone is open to meet new people. Outside Tsinghua, Chinese people are also open/welcoming. You'll see that it's very common to be social outside like at a park where you can play board games with random people or workout/dance in public (not that I joined it but it was nice to see people connecting in public since it's so different from Denmark).

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Do as much preparation as you can beforehand (figure out what apps you need to have set up to pay, to get around etc.).
Meet as many as you can/want but also settle into friend groups if that makes sense (for me going up to new people and trying to make new friends was out of my comfort zone, so just in general get out of your comfort zone)
Travel, and prepare yourself for where you want to go.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Maybe that Tsinghua is a closed area (big though!!) and you can't just enter if you're not a student/working there. So if you're bringing someone with you inside you need to give them visitation rights. If the person you're bringing is a local, the approval can be quick (like a few minutes) but if the person is international, it can take up to a few days. In my case I didn't know so I showed up on the first day with an uncle (who's a local) and my boyfriend (who was going to study at another university in Beijing) and I was only able to get my uncle in that day, but we were stopped in the process and it took a bit of time to get my uncle in. If I knew beforehand I could've set it up so both could get in with me smoothly. They're very strict at the gates!!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends I made.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Don't think there was one.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
